source.title: Predicting LLM Reasoning Performance with Small Proxy Model
source.authors: Woosung Koh; Juyoung Suk; Sung-Jun Han; Se-young Yun; Jamin Shin

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether proxy-model measurements predict downstream task performance at larger scales, using proxy-target correlations and prediction errors rather than the original held-out pretraining-loss scaling-law method.
record.gate_note: The study measures downstream benchmark accuracy/pass@1 and proxy-target predictability, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute. Its RBridge weighted NLL is a proxy evaluation score on frontier-model reasoning traces, not the held-out pretraining loss in V1. It also does not test a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Cited scaling-law claims and results from other work are not recorded as rows. The study's own small-model-versus-large-model downstream trends and proxy-target prediction results bear on V6.
record.test_reason: Figures 2 and 8 directly test V6 by measuring downstream accuracy across pretraining-token checkpoints at several model sizes. The main proxy-metric prediction experiments evaluate a different question: whether a specially constructed small-model evaluation score predicts larger-model accuracy.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors conclude that aligning proxy evaluation with the pretraining objective and target task improves prediction of larger-model reasoning accuracy, dataset ranking efficiency, and transfer to one alternative dataset. Their results concern proxy evaluation methods, alongside direct evidence that ordinary downstream accuracy can be noisy or decline at small scale.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a task-weighted NLL on frontier-model reasoning traces and cross-validated empirical proxy-to-target mappings, selecting among linear, quadratic, exponential, and logarithmic functions. It does not fit the original held-out pretraining-loss power laws or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Predictive relationship varies by benchmark, proxy metric, proxy/target scale, and whether target SFT is included. For MATH500 token-progress trends, the reported linear-fit R² is much lower for the 1B and 7B models than for 13B and 32B.

fits_no_version.finding: RBridge and comparator scores predict larger-model benchmark accuracy with varying cross-validated fit and error.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Task-aligned small-model evaluation scores can predict larger-model reasoning accuracy across matched training-token checkpoints.

fits_no_version.finding: The fitted RBridge mapping transfers to one alternative dataset with average error 2.490 percentage points and correct dataset ordering on five benchmarks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A task-specific proxy-to-target mapping can transfer across pretraining datasets at fixed training scale.

record.code_released: not stated; the authors say they open-sourced their dataset but provide no URL in the text
record.problems: The scale-to-downstream trend evidence is limited to the stated OLMo-based model sizes, one main pretraining dataset, and six benchmarks; the alternative-dataset transfer uses one additional dataset and 1B→7B models. The authors note that frontier models can produce incorrect or unformatted reasoning traces, and that they have not tested the method on long-CoT models. Some curve-fit results are shown in figures; the reported MATH500 R² values are legible.
record.rows_left_out: Not recorded: the <100M→1.2B dataset-ranking DAcc./compute-saving results, which concern ranking pretraining datasets rather than the scale-linked downstream-performance outcomes emphasized here; per-benchmark Table 3 transfer predictions and other proxy-method comparisons beyond the aggregate comparisons retained. Sections 4.2(i), Table 3, and Tables 2–6.

untested.parts: Held-out pretraining-loss power laws in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of small-run power laws to much larger runs' pretraining loss.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocations and their exponents.
Architecture changes at fixed parameter count.
Power-law forms beyond text pretraining, including fine-tuning and transfer.
Downstream performance versus held-out pretraining loss; generalization beyond the tested OLMo models, benchmarks, and token ranges.
Dependence of scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup and fitting choices; departures from a single loss power law.

missing.what: Direct benchmark-performance versus training-token curves for GSM8K, ARC-C, MMLU Pro, CQA, and HumanEval at 1B, 7B, 13B, and 32B. Record each curve's R² and readable direction; these show that predictability varies by benchmark and size, including among larger models.

record.verdict_notes: Numerical values in the extracted rows match the supplied text. Rows r01–r50 and r55–r56 should remain method-evaluation evidence outside these claim versions. Their specially constructed evaluation losses are not held-out pretraining loss, and their prediction errors should not be treated as scaling-law effect states. Cross-validation across token checkpoints does not establish extrapolation beyond the observed token range.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit of held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No test of whether small-run power laws predict much larger runs' held-out pretraining loss.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation sweep or fitted allocation exponents.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No tests of power-law forms across other modalities or the specified training regimes.

Tests are limited to downstream reasoning-benchmark measurements during pretraining and proxy-to-target prediction in the stated OLMo-based settings; it does not establish a general relationship between downstream performance and held-out pretraining loss.

The paper selects among specified curve families for proxy-target fitting, but does not test dependence of scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup, nor whether the claimed loss curves bend away from a power law.
